URL: https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/sep/23/tories-target-universal-credit-claimants-plan-condemned-fast-track-to-poverty
The Guardian — published Wed 23 September 2026 22:30 BST (2026-09-23T21:30:01Z); updated Thu 24 Sep 02:30 BST — Peter Walker

HEADLINE: Tories target universal credit claimants in plan condemned as 'fast track to poverty'
STANDFIRST: Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of living

FACTS:
- People claiming universal credit would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan.
- Those receiving this "subsistence allowance" would have it paid into a dedicated debit card preventing them from buying alcohol or tobacco — based on an Australian system that was scrapped after trials found limited evidence it changed behaviour.
- Under the plan, UC claimants would receive the full amount for six months; after that the sum would be tied to how long they have worked at a level that triggers national insurance payments. This would have to be for at least twice as long as the claimant period — so someone with two years of NI payments would qualify for another 12 months of full UC before falling to the lower rate.
- The lower rate is set at 70% of the standard amount. That would leave a single claimant aged under 25 living on £237 a month, or just over £7.50 a day. A couple aged 25 or over would lose £200 a month, falling to £466 in total.
- Anyone on the reduced level would have payments put on to a "back to work card" blocking purchases of alcohol, tobacco and gambling, and cash withdrawals.
- The plan excludes those already in work (about a third of UC claimants have jobs) and those assessed as having limited capability for work and work-related activity because of a health condition or disability. Separate payments for housing or dependent children would be unaffected.
- The Conservatives said the plan would affect about 350,000 people in England, Scotland and Wales and save £538m a year.
- The party cites Germany and the Netherlands, where unemployment payments are contribution-contingent and can be time-limited — though those payments are more generous (60–70% of previous monthly wage), and single people in Germany who have not paid in sufficiently receive about £480 a month.

QUOTE — KEMI BADENOCH, Conservative leader: the aim was to be "tough on those who exploit the system", adding: "Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered."

QUOTE — SARA OGILVIE, director of policy, Child Poverty Action Group: "The reality is that families are still paying the price of austerity cuts to our social security safety net. With living costs continuing to rise, these proposals are a fast track to increased poverty and are the last thing people need as they try to get back on their feet."

QUOTE — HELEN BARNARD, head of policy, Trussell: called the idea "deeply misguided", saying UC already had strong conditions to ensure people seek work. "If you're struggling to afford food and rent, childcare or the bus fare to an interview, then finding and keeping a job becomes harder not easier. Cutting support would only make things worse."

FRONT PAGES: This is the lead for The Times, The Daily Telegraph, the Daily Mail and the Daily Express on Thursday 24 September.
